talks.title: Demystifying Cloud Infrastructure Attacks
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Demystifying Cloud Infrastructure Attacks.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Alexander, a Principal Forensic Investigator at Truesec, deconstructs a complex, multi-stage hybrid cloud attack drawn from real-world incident response investigations. Tracing the intrusion backwards from an Azure/Entra ID tenant takeover to its initial root cause, he illustrates how threat actors chain developer machine compromises, Git repository supply-chain tampering, CI/CD container breakouts, and cloud credential harvesting. The presentation highlights the critical risks of hybrid identity infrastructure, demonstrating how on-premises Active Directory Connect servers can be weaponized to dominate enterprise cloud resources.

Key Topics:
- Hybrid identity architecture risks: ADFS Golden SAML, Pass-Through Authentication (PTA) skeleton keys, and Azure AD Connect Password Hash Sync (PHS) credential dumping
- CI/CD supply chain exploitation: Jenkins script console abuse, Docker default network container breakout, and malicious dependency tampering
- Covert Command and Control: living-off-the-cloud C2 tunneling via Gmail API drafts and attachments
- Cloud credential harvesting: GCP default service account storage bucket exposure, CLI SQLite database credential dumping, and DPAPI-based infostealers

Technical Details:
The incident investigation originated with an alert for single-factor authentication in Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), preceded by an unexpected password reset triggered by an on-premises Azure AD Connect service account (sync_*). In hybrid identity deployments utilizing Password Hash Sync (PHS), this internal service account possesses broad directory permissions, including the ability to reset user passwords to synchronize them between on-premises Active Directory and the cloud. By dumping these synced credentials from the on-premises AD Connect server (an activity typically detected by EDR as an AD Sync attack), the threat actor reset administrative passwords, assumed ownership of an Enterprise Application with delegated Microsoft Graph permissions (accessing mailboxes and SharePoint), promoted an account to Global Administrator, and enrolled a rogue device.

Lateral movement to the AD Connect server stemmed from a compromised Jenkins build automation server. The attacker accessed Jenkins' administrative Script Console to dump build secrets and execute arbitrary server commands. The server maintained persistent Command and Control (C2) through a custom RAT that communicated via the Gmail API: the malware polled a compromised Gmail account for new message drafts containing commands, executed them locally, and uploaded output as email attachments—effectively blending into legitimate outbound HTTPS traffic. This Jenkins host access was enabled by a network breakout from a Docker build container that had been placed on Docker's default bridge network, allowing it to route directly to the host's internal Jenkins web interface.

The initial breach began with a RedLine infostealer infection purchased on Russian Market, delivered via a spoofed GitHub issue attachment URL. The infostealer decrypted browser session cookies and Primary Refresh Tokens (PRTs) using Windows DPAPI on a developer's workstation. Stolen credentials allowed the attacker to access GitLab and modify a repository's requirements.txt, injecting a dependency that executed a reverse shell via setup.py during automated builds. Concurrently, the attacker compromised a Google Cloud Platform (GCP) development VM, querying the instance metadata service to hijack the default compute service account (which had read permissions over backup storage buckets containing administrative credentials) and dumping saved authentication tokens from local SQLite databases used by gcloud and Azure CLI tools.

Key Takeaways:
Hybrid identity infrastructure like Azure AD Connect represents a critical Tier-0 asset; compromising on-premises synchronization servers immediately grants complete administrative dominance over cloud tenants. Organizations must strictly segment CI/CD build environments, ensuring Docker containers cannot route to management consoles or internal networks, and audit pipelines against dependency tampering. Furthermore, enterprises should protect developer session tokens with hardware-backed TPM storage (such as Windows 11 PRT protection) and enforce Conditional Access policies requiring compliant, managed hardware for administrative logins.

talks.title: SBOMs for the Win! How PSIRT Teams Could Use SBOM
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning SBOMs for the Win! How PSIRT Teams Could Use SBOM.
talks.summary:
Schneider Electric Context

Harish Shankar and Fabrissa present Schneider Electric's product security program. The global energy and automation company operates across 100 countries with thousands of suppliers, integrators, and service partners, making supply-chain security critical.

End-to-End Security Program

Thirteen initiatives cover R&D through customer operations, adopting IEC 62443 standards, global security lab pen testing, source-code governance, secure manufacturing, tamper-proof staging, and field-engineer practices like banning unscanned USBs at customer sites.

SBOM Initiative

Fabrissa describes Schneider's SBOM program for firmware and embedded products with transitive dependencies. The journey began atop an existing product vulnerability management program where R&D teams already tracked component inventories.

PSIRT Integration

Software bill of materials is positioned as a key supply-chain security component enabling PSIRT teams to respond to vulnerabilities across complex products that blend operating systems, embedded software, and cloud components.

talks.title: Tales From a Cloud CSIRT- Let’s Deep Dive into a Kubernetes (k8s) Infection
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Tales From a Cloud CSIRT- Let’s Deep Dive into a Kubernetes (k8s) Infection.
talks.summary:
Incident Trigger

An Argentina-based responder describes a client whose public S3 static website suddenly showed access denied because objects were encrypted with a KMS key the tenant could no longer use. The case illustrates how fast-moving startups often skip logging and security prep.

CloudTrail Forensics

With no exported logs available, the team retrieved CloudTrail event history programmatically and built tooling to grep and analyze API activity. They traced suspicious get-authorization-token calls to ECR from an internal AWS address—unexpected for a user who should not touch the container registry.

Kubernetes and IAM Risk

The talk explains how Kubernetes service accounts mapped to IAM roles can give containers cluster-level cloud permissions without segmentation. Attackers who reach that trust boundary may push images, encrypt data, and abuse infrastructure-as-code patterns that provision users automatically.

Logging Gaps

AWS logs API calls via CloudTrail, but object-level S3 events are costly and usually off. Kubernetes adds API server, audit, authenticator, and controller logs that rarely get correlated with CloudTrail—leaving blind spots during cloud-native incidents.

talks.title: Cloud Console Cartographer: Tapping Into Mapping
talks.teaser: Slogging Thru Logging explores Cloud Console Cartographer: Tapping Into Mapping.
talks.summary:
Speakers and goal

Permiso researchers Cam and Daniel introduce Cloud Console Cartographer, an open-source tool to map noisy AWS console-session logs into understandable attacker or user activity.

Cloud logging realities

Cloud logs differ from endpoint telemetry: less control, API-call abstraction, control-plane vs data-plane split, retention limits (e.g., 30/90 days), delays, and query throttling. Forwarding to S3/blob storage helps scale and retention but can drop fields such as CloudTrail's resources section.

Console focus

Console means browser-based AWS/Azure portal use, not CLI. They say attackers do use consoles, sometimes with click-through playbooks or technical limitations.

Defender guidance

Enable non-default logs, forward them to durable storage, monitor ingestion, and test tools before incidents. The talk promises a solution walkthrough and demo of Cartographer for reconstructing what happened inside verbose console sessions.

talks.title: One Chain to Shackle Them All
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning One Chain to Shackle Them All.
talks.summary:
## Supply Chain as Permanent Risk

A Siemens product-security veteran presents "One Chain to Shackle Them All" at FIRST, arguing software supply chains create a never-ending vulnerability chain shackling vendors and consumers alike. Managing over 10,000 products, his team disclosed roughly a thousand vulnerabilities last year—manual scale impossible to sustain through automation alone.

## Two-Party Models Fail

CVSS environmental scores, legal vendor-customer contracts, and SSVC decision frameworks assume binary relationships. Real supply chains contain many hops: component authors, integrators, OEMs, distributors, and end operators. Vulnerabilities propagate instantly downstream while patches travel slowly upstream.

## Patch Propagation Asymmetry

Illustrative timelines show fixes taking months per hop—potentially over two years from initial disclosure to final deployer. Meanwhile exploit knowledge spreads immediately. Organizations still patching 2022 flaws while attackers chain current CVEs exemplify systemic lag no single vendor can solve.

## Toward Collective Accountability

The speaker urges industry-wide coordination: transparent dependency graphs, synchronized disclosure windows, and realistic expectations that "just automate patching" ignores integration testing, safety certification, and OT downtime constraints. Supply-chain security requires multi-stakeholder mechanisms, not bilateral SLAs.
